Pronunciation note for this grammar point:
The relative pronoun is unstressed unless it is the subject, and the clause after a comma drops in pitch, which is how a listener hears that the information is an aside rather than a definition.
Read it aloud, then record yourself: the main stress falls on the content word, not on the hedge.

elements.content: Grammar focus: Relative Clauses: Review and Deepening.

Decide first whether the clause identifies (no commas, that allowed) or adds (commas, that forbidden). Then choose the pronoun by its role inside the clause, not in the main sentence. Finally, cut: if the pronoun is the object, delete it; if the clause is passive or progressive, reduce it to a participle.

who / that — person, subject: the analyst who wrote the note
which / that — thing, subject or object: the report that we commissioned
whose — possessive: the consultant whose figures we used
where / when — place or time adverbial: the office where the audit took place
preposition + which — formal, replaces a stranded preposition: the cost of which we spoke
reduced clause — participle replaces the pronoun and verb: the report commissioned last year
Guided practice: choose the correct option.
1. Complete: 'The office ___ the audit took place is closed.'
2. Complete: 'The consultant ___ figures we used has resigned.'
3. Which sentence needs no comma?
options: The report which we commissioned has arrived.
The report, which we commissioned, has arrived.

elements.content: Read and listen: three examples in context.

The analyst who wrote the note — has left the team. (Defining: identifies which analyst.)
The note, which was leaked, — caused an outcry. (Non-defining: adds information.)
The cost of which we spoke — has doubled. (Preposition plus which in formal register.)
What do you observe?

A defining clause tells you which noun is meant and takes no commas: the report that we commissioned. A non-defining clause adds information and takes commas: the report, which we commissioned, has arrived. That never follows a comma; which can. Whose replaces a possessive, where replaces a place adverbial, and preposition + which replaces a prepositional phrase at the end of a formal clause.
1. Which clause can take commas?
2. Can the relative pronoun be dropped in 'the report that we commissioned'?
options: Yes: it is the object of the clause.

elements.content: State the rule in one sentence, without looking at the table.
Freer production: I can describe people and things without repeating their names.

Success criteria:
- I can keep defining and non-defining clauses apart.
- I can choose whose, where and preposition + which.
- I can reduce a relative clause to a participle.
Role play: put your position in ninety seconds; your partner notes every use of the target structure.
Frequent errors and correction:

❌ The report, that we commissioned, has arrived (that after a comma) → ✅ The report, which we commissioned, has arrived
❌ The analyst who he wrote the note has left (pronoun and subject both kept) → ✅ The analyst who wrote the note has left
Correct these sentences: say what is wrong, then give the right version.
Acceptable variants:

The figures collected in March are now suspect.
The chair, whose term ends in May, will not stand again.
The meeting at which the decision was taken was not minuted.
